notes.meaning: After the deadly plague at Peor, the Lord spoke directly to Moses and to Aaron's son Eleazar. Aaron had recently died, so Eleazar now stood in his father's place as high priest. This command marked a major turning point, showing that the older generation had completely passed away and a new generation was ready to enter the promised land.

God told Moses and Eleazar to count every man twenty years old or older who was able to fight in Israel's army. This census would show God's faithfulness in multiplying Abraham's descendants despite forty years of judgment in the wilderness. It was also ordered so the land of Canaan could later be divided fairly among the tribes based on their size.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars see these large census totals as symbolic or idealized figures, arguing that the wilderness could not have sustained a population of around two million people.

notes.meaning: Moses and Eleazar delivered the Lord's instructions while camped on the plains of Moab across the Jordan River from Jericho. Israel was now right on the threshold of Canaan, and the long wandering was over. Moses gathered and counted the adult men under God's explicit command, just as he had done decades earlier at Mount Sinai.

The enrollment began with Reuben, Jacob's firstborn son, listing the four primary clans descended from him. The fighting men of Reuben totaled 43,730. This was a drop of nearly three thousand men since the first census, showing the lingering cost of past rebellions among their families.

The family record specifically traces Pallu's line down to Eliab's sons, including Dathan and Abiram. These two men were respected tribal leaders, but they used their positions to join Korah in an uprising against Moses and Aaron. By opposing the leaders God had appointed, they were actually fighting against the Lord Himself.

God judged those rebels by causing the earth to split open and swallow them up, while fire consumed the two hundred and fifty men offering incense. Their sudden death stood as an enduring warning sign to all future generations. It proved that rebellion against God's order always leads to ruin.

Even though Korah was destroyed, his children did not die with him. They chose not to join their father's sin and were spared from his punishment. God showed great mercy to them, and their descendants later served faithfully as musicians and writers of many Psalms in God's temple.

Simeon's descendants were grouped into five main clans, totaling 22,200 men of military age. Simeon suffered the greatest loss of any tribe, shrinking by more than half since Mount Sinai. Many of their men had likely been struck down in the recent plague after a Simeonite leader led people into Baal worship.

The tribe of Gad was registered according to its seven main family clans. These clans matched the original sons of Gad who went down to Egypt centuries before. God had preserved each family line through forty difficult years in the desert.

The registered soldiers in the clans of Gad numbered 40,500 men. Gad also experienced a loss of over five thousand men compared to the first census. Still, they remained a strong and capable force ready to take their place in Israel's army.

Judah's first two sons, Er and Onan, had died long before in the land of Canaan because the Lord judged their wickedness. Because they died childless before Israel entered Egypt, they formed no family branches in the tribe. This note explains why their names do not appear in the tribal clan list.

Judah's living descendants came through his son Shelah and his twin sons Perez and Zerah. The line of Perez was so fruitful that it split into two large sub-clans named after his sons Hezron and Hamul. God showed rich grace by growing a mighty family out of Judah despite earlier sorrow and sin.

Judah's fighting men numbered 76,500, making it the largest tribe in all of Israel. While the first three tribes listed had shrunk during the desert years, Judah grew by nearly two thousand men. This rapid growth reflected God's ancient promise that Judah would be a praised and leading tribe.
